title: Past, Present, and Future of Decision Support Technology
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.
access: Complete source PDF in GitHub checkout; relevant text sections inspected.
author: Shim, Warkentin, Courtney, Power, Sharda & Carlsson
problem: Classical individual DSS had limited database, modeling and interface functions; networked organizations also need collaborative and interorganizational support.
method: Historical/technical narrative synthesis based on an invited panel; reviews data warehousing, OLAP, data mining, Web-based support, collaboration and optimization.
data: Illustrative DSS technologies and organizational arrangements, including virtual teams; no single benchmark dataset or new controlled deployment study.
findings: DSS capabilities broadened through both technical and organizational developments. Databases, models and interfaces remain complementary; wider reach introduces communication and coordination requirements.
limitations: Inferred: historical description and forecasts do not isolate causal adoption effects. Selected examples are not a representative sample of organizations, and predictions made in 2002 are not verified outcomes.
future: Author-discussed: mobile/wireless support, active decision support and collaboration. Suggested: longitudinal tests of whether integration improves coordinated decisions.
locator: Journal pp 111–118; p 116 analytical demand; pp 117–122 collaboration/Web discussion.

title: Specifying an Expanded Framework for Classifying and Describing Decision Support Systems
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.
access: Complete source PDF in GitHub checkout; relevant text sections inspected.
author: Power
problem: Overlapping labels such as BI, expert systems, group DSS and Web DSS make systems difficult to classify or compare consistently.
method: Conceptual framework with one primary dimension (dominant technology) and three secondary dimensions (target users, purpose and deployment/enabling technology).
data: Examples of communications-, data-, document-, knowledge- and model-driven DSS; mainframe, spreadsheet, client/server and Web deployments. No empirical benchmark.
findings: Five DSS types can serve different users and purposes across deployment architectures. A Web interface or a group audience is not itself a distinct analytical method.
limitations: Inferred: a taxonomy does not establish comparative effectiveness, adoption frequency or a universal historical sequence; hybrid systems can span categories.
future: Suggested: test classification agreement and usefulness on modern hybrid DSS, and separate deployment architecture from decision purpose in empirical comparisons.
locator: Journal pp 158–164; p 162 communications-driven/group support.

title: Models and Managers: The Concept of a Decision Calculus
version: MIT Sloan Working Paper 403-69, June 1969; version cited in the uploaded review.
access: Complete archival/publisher working copy; not present in checked GitHub PDF folder.
author: Little
problem: Managerial models may be technically sophisticated yet unused because managers cannot understand, control or adapt them to their decisions.
method: Design argument for a decision calculus: simple, robust, controllable, adaptive, sufficiently complete models with an accessible interface; illustrates iterative manager–model use.
data: ADBUDG II advertising-budget model then in trial use by three product managers; additional practitioner/modeling anecdotes. Assessed 1969 MIT working-paper version.
findings: Usability, judgment and controllability matter alongside numerical capability. Adding detail to overcome distrust can make a model less understandable; interaction can expose input errors.
limitations: Inferred: small illustrative trial and anecdotes do not identify causal organizational benefits. Judgmental inputs and simplified assumptions limit transfer to other decisions.
future: Suggested: compare model complexity, understandability and decision outcomes with larger manager samples; test sensitivity to uncertain inputs and longitudinal adaptation.
locator: Scan PDF p 9 abstract; pp 11–23 design/interface discussion; p 29 onward ADBUDG II.

title: A Framework for Management Information Systems
version: MIT Sloan Working Paper 510-71, February 1971; version cited in the uploaded review.
access: Complete archival/publisher working copy; not present in checked GitHub PDF folder.
author: Gorry & Scott Morton
problem: Growing computer/MIS investment had not consistently improved managerial decisions; system designs often failed to distinguish different decision and information requirements.
method: Conceptual framework relating strategic planning, management control and operational control to structured and less-structured decision activities and their information needs.
data: Analytical framework and managerial examples; no new experimental dataset. Assessed MIT Working Paper 510-71, February 1971, rather than later journal pagination.
findings: Interactive technology and understanding of decision processes jointly enable support. Strategic information needs differ in character, not just aggregation; selective information or sampling may be appropriate.
limitations: Author-stated scope: a static framework, not a systems-implementation process model. Inferred: it does not measure adoption effects or validate one architecture for all organizations.
future: Suggested: test the framework through comparative organizational deployments and follow changes in decision structure, information needs and support arrangements over time.
locator: Scan PDF pp 7–11 introduction; pp 13–25 framework; p 25 sampling/detail; p 29 decision structure.

title: The Evolution of Decision Support Systems (DSS) to Strategic AI: A Systematic Review of Architectural Shifts and Business Value
version: RIGGS 5(1), pp 8905–8916, published 23 March 2026.
access: Complete archival/publisher working copy; not present in checked GitHub PDF folder.
author: Budianto, Lubis, Mukti & Budianto
problem: Architectural accounts of DSS and management accounts of strategic AI are fragmented; the links between autonomy, organizational change and business value need synthesis.
method: Authors report a PRISMA-oriented systematic literature review and propose a DSS–Strategic AI convergence framework linking architecture, autonomy, governance and strategic value.
data: Authors report 85 included publications from Scopus, Web of Science and IEEE Xplore covering 2000–2025. This is the paper’s reported corpus, not an independently reproduced search.
findings: Proposes an architectural/value progression and discusses orchestration, monitoring, technical debt, drift and governance latency. These are conceptual relationships, not newly estimated business-value effects.
limitations: Inferred: the visible PDF does not provide a record-level 85-study list sufficient to reproduce its selection. Architectural causation/value claims remain conceptual; the review is not a controlled adoption study.
future: Author-discussed: empirical validation of the proposed convergence framework. Suggested: compare autonomy and governance changes with actual decision outcomes and counterexamples.
locator: pp 8905–8907 abstract/method/Table 2; pp 8908–8912 architecture/feedback; p 8914 conclusion.

title: Decision Support Systems: Evolution, Architectures, Applications, and Future Directions
version: Data Intelligence and Informatics Practice 1(1), pp 19–31, published 2026.
access: Complete archival/publisher working copy; not present in checked GitHub PDF folder.
author: Eze, Bello & Akinyemi
problem: DSS research spans different taxonomies, architectures and domains, making an integrated account of capabilities, implementation risks and future development difficult.
method: Structured integrative literature review; synthesizes taxonomy, architecture, applications and governance and proposes a divergent–convergent workflow with human decision gates and feedback.
data: Authors describe 40 selected empirical/theoretical works across 1971–2024, with foundational material; application examples span healthcare, finance, supply chains and public administration.
findings: Positions contemporary DSS as hybrid combinations of data, models, knowledge and collaboration. Proposes iterative problem structuring, analytical branching, integration and monitoring rather than a single algorithm.
limitations: Inferred: proposed workflow is not independently validated. Broad accuracy/time/satisfaction values in Table 2 lack a demonstrated common benchmark and should not be treated as comparable pooled effects.
future: Author-discussed: adaptive support, interoperability, explainability, accountability and longitudinal human-factor evaluation. Suggested: validate the proposed workflow against simpler domain-specific baselines.
locator: pp 20–23 review method, taxonomy and architecture; pp 25–27 process model/research agenda.

title: The Art of Artificial Intelligence: Themes and Case Studies of Knowledge Engineering
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.
access: Complete source PDF in GitHub checkout; relevant text sections inspected.
author: Feigenbaum
problem: Expert-level scientific and medical reasoning requires domain knowledge that generic search procedures or computation alone cannot supply.
method: Invited knowledge-engineering synthesis using project descriptions to explain acquiring expertise, representing it, constructing inference and explaining reasoning.
data: PUFF pulmonary-function interpretation; DENDRAL chemical inference and MYCIN-related clinical knowledge engineering. Illustrative project cases, not one common experimental dataset.
findings: Domain knowledge and its representation are central to expert performance. Knowledge engineering makes expertise operational, while elicitation, explanation and control remain technical and practical tasks.
limitations: Inferred: selected project descriptions do not establish general organizational effectiveness. Narrow domain scope and knowledge acquisition/maintenance restrict transfer and scaling.
future: Suggested: evaluate knowledge acquisition and update costs, handling of exceptions, explanation usefulness and combinations with learned models in actual decision workflows.
locator: Proceedings pp 1014–1017 opening examples and knowledge-engineering argument; later knowledge/uncertainty discussion.

title: Expert System Methodologies and Applications: A Decade Review from 1995 to 2004
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.

author: Liao
problem: Expert-system methods and application domains expanded rapidly, requiring an organized view of development patterns rather than treating expert systems as a single method.
method: Literature review/classification using keywords and article abstracts; categorizes methodologies into 11 groups, including rules, knowledge-based systems, neural/fuzzy methods, cases, agents and ontologies.
data: 166 articles in 78 journals, retrieved from five online databases, covering 1995–2004; methodological/application categories rather than a shared performance dataset.
findings: Expert-system methods diversify and are often domain/problem oriented. The article identifies continuing knowledge change and integration with other perspectives as development themes.
limitations: Inferred: keyword/abstract selection and a bounded period limit coverage. Counts of methods/publications are not comparable estimates of system accuracy, adoption or decision benefit.
future: Author-stated: expertise orientation; applications informed by psychology, cognitive science and behavior; continued change and new understanding as drivers of expert systems.
locator: Abstract; Secs 1–2 review/classification; discussion and conclusion.

title: Preference Learning and Multiple Criteria Decision Aiding: Differences, Commonalities, and Synergies—Part I
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.
access: Complete source PDF in GitHub checkout; relevant text sections inspected.
author: Hüllermeier & Słowiński
problem: MCDA and preference learning share decision-modeling goals but developed in different communities with different assumptions, terminology and success criteria.
method: Conceptual invited survey; Part I reviews multiple-criteria decision aiding and preference representation to prepare a comparison with preference learning in the companion Part II.
data: Formal decision models, criteria, alternatives, choice/ranking/classification examples and MCDA approaches; no single benchmark dataset or new comparative effectiveness experiment.
findings: MCDA can support an individual or a defined group; multiple criteria do not imply multiple participants. Explicit preferences and data-driven preference learning offer complementary modeling possibilities.
limitations: Scope: Part I alone is not the complete two-part MCDA/PL comparison. Inferred: the survey does not demonstrate that one preference method improves decisions across domains or resolves value conflicts.
future: Author-stated aim: stimulate research at the intersection of MCDA and PL. Suggested: compare elicitation burden, stability and treatment of noncompensatory or conflicting preferences with real decision makers.
locator: Abstract; p 180 Sec 1; pp 182–183 Sec 2.1; subsequent MCDA modeling sections.

title: An Overview of Data Warehousing and OLAP Technology
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.

author: Chaudhuri & Dayal
problem: Operational databases are optimized for transactions, while organizational analysis needs integrated histories, complex queries and consistent cross-functional information.
method: Technical overview of warehouse/OLAP architecture, extraction/cleaning/integration, refresh, metadata, multidimensional analysis, materialized views, indexing and query processing.
data: Illustrative OLTP/OLAP workloads and enterprise versus departmental data architectures; historical scale descriptions, not a new controlled organizational dataset.

limitations: Inferred: architectural rationale is not a measured causal estimate of business benefit. Data quality, shared meaning and integration work persist;1997 workload descriptions are not current benchmarks.
future: Suggested: measure total integration/maintenance and user-decision costs, compare federated and enterprise arrangements, and evaluate incremental refresh and shared metadata in context.

title: From Data Mining to Knowledge Discovery in Databases
authors: Usama Fayyad; Gregory Piatetsky-Shapiro; Padhraic Smyth
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.

author: Fayyad, Piatetsky-Shapiro & Smyth
problem: Collected data can exceed human capacity to discover useful, valid and understandable patterns; applying a mining algorithm alone does not complete knowledge discovery.
method: Defines KDD and distinguishes it from data mining; presents an iterative process of domain understanding, selection, preprocessing, transformation, mining, interpretation and evaluation.
data: Illustrative scientific/business applications, including SKICAT astronomical object classification and examples in fraud, finance and manufacturing; no unified benchmark cohort.
findings: Useful knowledge depends on a multistep human/technical process rather than raw data volume or algorithm performance alone. Iteration can revise the data, goals and representations.
limitations: Inferred: examples and a process framework do not establish a common causal outcome across applications. Validity, scaling, data quality and interpretation remain context dependent.

title: Random Forests
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.
access: Complete source PDF in GitHub checkout; relevant text sections inspected.
author: Breiman
problem: Single trees and correlated ensemble errors limit predictive performance; ensemble construction needs to balance individual-tree strength and dependence.
method: Randomized tree ensemble with bagging and random feature selection; theoretical generalization analysis plus out-of-bag estimates, noise experiments and predictive comparisons.
data: UCI classification datasets, larger held-out tasks and synthetic data; random forests, AdaBoost/bagging comparisons, out-of-bag error and variable-importance estimates.
findings: The theoretical limiting error relates to tree strength and correlation. Reported experiments show competitive prediction and robustness under tested noise conditions; OOB estimates support internal monitoring.
limitations: Inferred: benchmark prediction is not a test of organizational decision utility, fairness or causal validity. More trees alone do not correct unsuitable features, labels or distribution shift.
future: Suggested: evaluate calibration, distribution shift, correlated inputs, domain-specific decision costs and resource/interpretability trade-offs rather than extrapolating benchmark accuracy alone.
locator: Abstract; Secs 1–3 theory/OOB; Secs 5–8 experiments, noise and interpretation.

title: Machine Learning: Trends, Perspectives, and Prospects
authors: Michael I. Jordan; Tom M. Mitchell

author: Jordan & Mitchell
problem: Rapid growth in learning algorithms, online data and inexpensive computation creates opportunities and unresolved questions about constructing systems that improve from experience.

data: Examples across healthcare, manufacturing, education, finance and other domains; no newly assembled common dataset or controlled organizational intervention.

title: Deep Learning
authors: Yann LeCun; Yoshua Bengio; Geoffrey Hinton
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.

author: LeCun, Bengio & Hinton
problem: Hand-engineered features restrict conventional learning on raw images, speech and other high-dimensional signals; useful representations are difficult to design manually.
method: Review of multilayer representation learning, backpropagation, convolutional and recurrent networks, and developments supported by data and computation.
data: Examples from vision, speech, language, genomics and drug discovery; benchmark results reviewed from other work, not a new single DSS dataset.

title: Why Should I Trust You? Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier
authors: Marco Tulio Ribeiro; Sameer Singh; Carlos Guestrin
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.
access: Complete source PDF in GitHub checkout; relevant text sections inspected.
author: Ribeiro, Singh & Guestrin
problem: High held-out accuracy can conceal spurious features or deployment failure; users need to understand individual predictions and judge whether a model should be trusted.
method: LIME perturbs an input and fits a locally weighted interpretable surrogate; SP-LIME selects representative explanations using a submodular coverage objective.
data: Text and image classifiers, simulated trust/feature experiments and human-subject tasks; examples include 20 Newsgroups-related classification and image superpixels.
findings: Local explanations can expose reliance on misleading features and assist model inspection/selection in the studied tasks. Representative examples can broaden inspection beyond one prediction.
limitations: Inferred: local surrogate fidelity is not global or causal validity. Results depend on perturbations, neighborhood, representation and the user task; an explanation does not certify safe deployment.
future: Author-discussed: extend interpretation methods and evaluate human/model interaction. Suggested: test stability, realistic perturbations, calibrated trust and decision outcomes in target domains.
locator: Abstract; Secs 2–4 LIME/SP-LIME; Sec 5 evaluations; Sec 8 future work.
design: Method paper with computational and human evaluations

title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.
access: Complete source PDF in GitHub checkout; relevant text sections inspected.
author: Lundberg & Lee
problem: Feature-explanation methods use different definitions and can disagree, complicating interpretation of complex predictive models.
method: Unifies additive feature-attribution methods through Shapley values; derives local accuracy, missingness and consistency properties and develops Kernel SHAP and model-specific approximations.
data: Synthetic/explanation tasks, dense/sparse decision-tree examples, human-intuition comparisons and a convolutional classifier on MNIST; comparisons with LIME and DeepLIFT.
findings: Under the stated additive-attribution framework, a unique solution satisfies the proposed properties. Approximation methods improve sample efficiency/consistency in the reported tests.
limitations: Inferred: attribution explains a model relative to a background/reference distribution, not causality. Conditional expectations, correlated inputs and approximation assumptions affect interpretations; not a DSS effectiveness trial.
future: Author-discussed: common interpretation principles can guide future methods. Suggested: examine dependent features, baseline sensitivity, approximation error and user decision quality.
locator: Secs 2–4 additive properties/estimators; Sec 5 experiments; Sec 6 conclusion.

title: Attention Is All You Need
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.

author: Vaswani et al.
problem: Recurrent sequence models constrain training parallelism and make long-range dependencies difficult to handle efficiently.
method: Transformer encoder/decoder built from self-attention, multi-head attention, position representations and feed-forward layers, without recurrence/convolution in the proposed model.
data: WMT 2014 English–German and English–French translation; parsing transfer; base/big models trained on eight P100 GPUs under reported schedules.
findings: The big model reports 28.4 BLEU on English–German after about 3.5 days on eight P100 GPUs. Demonstrates an architecture/resource interaction in sequence tasks, not organizational DSS outcomes.
limitations: Inferred: translation/parsing benchmarks do not establish decision validity or adoption causes. The inspected revision has inconsistent English–French values across prose and abstract/table; that metric is not used here.
future: Author-discussed: apply attention architectures to other modalities and improve efficient/local attention. Suggested: compare quality, cost and latency under decision-specific workloads.

title: Language Models Are Few-Shot Learners
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.
access: Complete source PDF in GitHub checkout; relevant text sections inspected.
author: Brown et al.
problem: Task-specific fine-tuning often requires many labeled examples and a new adaptation pipeline for every NLP task.
method: Train autoregressive GPT-3 models at increasing scale and evaluate zero-, one- and few-shot prompting without gradient updates during downstream task evaluation.
data: Up to 175 billion parameters; mixed Web/book/Wikipedia pretraining; translation, QA, cloze, reading-comprehension, arithmetic and other NLP benchmarks.
findings: Scaling improves many few-shot results and task reuse, while performance remains uneven across tasks. In-context demonstrations can specify tasks without task-specific parameter updates.
limitations: Author-discussed: benchmark contamination, weak tasks, bias/misuse and difficulty separating learning from memorization. Inferred: NLP accuracy does not establish robust managerial decisions or low serving costs.
future: Suggested: improve data/contamination auditing, resource efficiency, robustness, multilingual coverage and independent decision-task evaluation; study when adaptation requires more than prompting.
locator: Abstract; Sec 2 models/training/evaluation; Sec 3 results; Sec 4 contamination; Sec 5 limitations.

title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.
access: Complete source PDF in GitHub checkout; relevant text sections inspected.
author: Wei et al.
problem: Standard prompting underuses some large language models on arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning tasks.
method: Few-shot chain-of-thought prompting supplies exemplars with intermediate reasoning steps; compares with standard prompting and ablations across model scales without task fine-tuning.
data: GSM8K and other arithmetic tasks, commonsense benchmarks and symbolic tasks; PaLM 540B example uses eight reasoning exemplars. Text prompts and outputs are the intervention.
findings: Reasoning-step exemplars improve reported task performance, particularly in sufficiently large models. This is a prompting strategy, not a new network architecture or guarantee of correct reasoning.
limitations: Author-stated: correct answers can arise from faulty reasoning; exemplar creation and large-model serving are costly; generalization and faithfulness remain open. Results are benchmark/model specific.
future: Author-discussed: induce reasoning in smaller models, improve factual reasoning and reduce exemplar costs. Suggested: test independently validated reasoning under real decision constraints.
locator: Secs 3–5 task studies; Sec 6 discussion/limitations; Sec 8 conclusion. Checked arXiv v6(2023), NeurIPS 2022 work.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.
access: Complete source PDF in GitHub checkout; relevant text sections inspected.
author: Lewis et al.
problem: Knowledge encoded only in model parameters is difficult to update, access precisely or inspect for provenance in knowledge-intensive generation.
method: Retrieval-augmented generation combines a pretrained sequence-to-sequence generator with a dense retriever and nonparametric Wikipedia passage index; compares sequence-level and token-level formulations.
data: Wikipedia index; open-domain QA and knowledge-intensive language tasks, including Natural Questions, TriviaQA, WebQuestions and fact-verification settings.
findings: Retrieval/generation improves several tested knowledge-intensive tasks. Index replacement demonstrates bounded knowledge updating without retraining the generator; retrieved passages offer inspectable evidence.
limitations: Inferred: retrieval may miss relevant evidence or return misleading passages; an available passage/citation does not verify every generated claim. Wikipedia tasks do not establish organizational access-control or decision performance.
future: Suggested: test domain-specific/current corpora, retrieval coverage, citation entailment, contradictory evidence, permission boundaries and cost/latency separately from answer accuracy.
locator: Abstract; Secs 1–2 architecture/Fig 1; task evaluations; Sec 4.5 knowledge updating. Checked arXiv v4(2021) of 2020 work.

title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.
access: Complete source PDF in GitHub checkout; relevant text sections inspected.
author: Yao et al.
problem: Language-model reasoning and action generation are often studied separately; unsupported internal reasoning can propagate errors without external observations.
method: ReAct interleaves language reasoning traces with task-specific actions and observations; uses demonstrations and available environment/API actions rather than only a one-shot answer.
data: HotpotQA and FEVER with Wikipedia interaction; ALFWorld household simulation and WebShop shopping tasks; compares reasoning-only/action-only and other tested baselines.
findings: External observations can help update plans and reduce unsupported reasoning. Reported interactive-task gains are specific to the evaluated demonstrations, models, environments and baselines.
limitations: Author-discussed: useful reasoning/action trajectories are hard to obtain and improve. Inferred: benchmark tool use is not a guarantee of execution safety, faithful explanations or long-horizon reliability.
future: Author-discussed: scale training/fine-tuning and improve human interaction with reasoning/action trajectories. Suggested: validate permissions, failure recovery, plan constraints and realistic deployment cost.
locator: Abstract; Sec 2 approach; Sec 3 QA/fact verification; Sec 4 interactive tasks; discussion.

title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.
access: Complete source PDF in GitHub checkout; relevant text sections inspected.
author: Schick et al.
problem: Language models can be fluent yet weak at arithmetic, factual lookup and current information that specialized tools can provide.
method: Self-supervised tool-use training: sample candidate API calls, execute them, retain calls that improve next-token loss, and fine-tune on text augmented with tool calls/results.
data: GPT-J-based model and a CCNet subset; calculator, QA, search, translation and calendar tools; downstream factual, arithmetic, QA and language-modeling tasks.
findings: A smaller tool-augmented model improves zero-shot results on tested tasks and can compete with larger baselines in some settings. Tool interfaces change available capabilities rather than only increasing parameter count.
limitations: Author-stated: independently generated tool calls cannot chain tools or support interactive browsing/refined searches; results depend on prompt wording, calculator sampling can be inefficient, and tool-specific computational costs are not modeled. Inferred: task results do not establish reliable autonomous organizational decisions.
future: Suggested from the stated limitations: evaluate chained and interactive tool use, cost-aware selection, prompt robustness and failure recovery in decision workflows.
locator: Abstract; Secs 2–3 call sampling/execution/filtering; experimental tasks; discussion/limitations. Checked arXiv v1(2023).

author: Wu et al.
problem: Complex LLM applications require reusable coordination among model calls, tools, code and people, beyond isolated prompt engineering.
method: AutoGen provides customizable conversable agents and conversation programming; agents can combine language models, human input and tool execution under configurable interaction/termination rules.
data: Six demonstration/evaluation applications: mathematics, retrieval-augmented chat, ALFWorld, OptiGuide multi-agent coding, dynamic group chat and conversational chess; model/tool configurations vary by application.

title: Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.

author: Madaan et al.
problem: A language model’s first output is often improvable, but collecting supervised revisions or training a separate feedback model can be costly.
method: Self-Refine uses the same model to generate an answer, produce actionable feedback and iteratively revise it; no additional parameter training is required by the procedure.
data: Seven tasks: dialogue, code optimization/readability, math, sentiment reversal, acronym generation and constrained generation; GPT-3.5/ChatGPT/GPT-4/Codex variants, human and automatic evaluation.

future: Author-discussed: broader model/task application and follow-up refinement research. Suggested: test open/smaller models, multilingual settings, stopping rules, budget-matched baselines and external validators.

title: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.
access: Complete source PDF in GitHub checkout; relevant text sections inspected.
author: Dean & Ghemawat
problem: Large computations require partitioning, scheduling, data movement and fault handling across many machines, obscuring otherwise simple application logic.
method: MapReduce programming model plus a cluster runtime: map/reduce functions, automatic partitioning, scheduling, locality, worker re-execution and backup tasks for slow workers.
data: Reported cluster of about 1800 machines; approximately 1-TB grep/sort workloads and runtime experiments. The inspected implementation does not transparently recover every failure type.
findings: In the reported sort experiment, completion took 891 seconds with backup tasks and 1283 seconds without (about 44% more elapsed time). Architecture/execution policy affects usable throughput alongside available hardware.
limitations: Author-stated implementation scope includes aborting on master failure. Inferred: batch throughput does not imply low-latency interactive suitability, equal resource consumption or better organizational decisions.
future: Suggested: compare scheduling, resource cost and failure recovery under interactive/streaming as well as batch workloads; measure integration costs before adopting the execution model in DSS.
locator: Secs 2–3 model/implementation; Sec 5.1 environment; Secs 5.2–5.4 grep/sort and backup-task experiments.

title: Eight Key Issues for the Decision Support Systems Discipline
version: Version in the GitHub PDF; preprint revision identified in access sheet when applicable.
access: Complete source PDF in GitHub checkout; relevant text sections inspected.
author: Arnott & Pervan
problem: DSS research risks losing relevance and coherence when technical artifacts, decision theory, funding and organizational practice are weakly connected.
method: Synthesizes a long-term content-analysis program and derives eight disciplinary issues; explains journal selection, coding, calibration and interpretation of research relevance.
data: 1,093 DSS articles in 14 major journals,1990–2004; research publications and coded categories, not an adoption or system-performance dataset.
findings: Identifies professional relevance, methods/paradigms, judgment theory, artifact roles, funding, agenda inertia, journal exposure and coherence as key issues. Research publication trends do not directly measure practical effectiveness.
limitations: Inferred: journal/time-window selection and interpretive relevance coding limit generalization. Findings concern the sampled research field and should not be applied as current prevalence or effectiveness statistics.
future: Author-stated: more context-sensitive case/design-science research, stronger theoretical foundations and professional relevance, industry engagement/funding and attention to BI/warehousing.
locator: pp 657–662 abstract/methods/relevance/theory; p 667 and concluding research recommendations.
design: Empirical content analysis and disciplinary synthesis
